title: Indian Diaspora Could Pay Price for West's Immigration Backlash, Sareen Warns
excerpt: Speaking on Faultline, Sushant Sareen said communities with a long record of legal migration and integration could still be caught by visa tightening and scrutiny aimed at migration in general.
body:
• Strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen has warned that the West's growing anti-immigration backlash could spill onto the Indian diaspora, even though Indian communities have a long record of legal migration and integration.
  • The warning, made on the Faultline programme with host Ananya Dasgupta, follows President Donald Trump attributing civil unrest in France to immigration and urging President Emmanuel Macron to tighten borders — a claim Macron pushed back on.
  • Sareen pointed to Canada, where he alleged criminal activity linked to some factions, including Khalistani networks, has begun to tarnish the image of the wider Indian community.
  • For Indians abroad and those planning to move: the practical risk he identifies is blunter visa scrutiny and policy tightening aimed at migration in general, not at Indians specifically — worth tracking in your country of residence or destination.

Rising anti-immigration sentiment across Western countries could have unintended consequences for the Indian diaspora, strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen has warned. Speaking on the programme Faultline with host Ananya Dasgupta, Sareen said law-abiding immigrants may face stricter scrutiny and backlash as political leaders in the West increasingly link social unrest to migration policy, Mirror Now reported.

The debate sharpened after US President Donald Trump attributed civil unrest in France to immigration and urged French President Emmanuel Macron to tighten national borders. Macron pushed back, suggesting outside figures were exploiting domestic tensions for political leverage. The Faultline episode, titled "Who Failed France?", asks whether immigration is the real problem or whether immigrants are becoming scapegoats for deeper economic, social and political failures, and examines the backlash across the United States, France and Britain, alongside the different models of Poland and Hungary, according to the programme's description on YouTube.

The risk Sareen identifies

Sareen noted that the Indian diaspora has historically maintained a strong reputation for success and integration in countries such as the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. His caution was that this standing is increasingly vulnerable to broader anti-migrant trends: when politics turns against migration in general, communities that arrived legally and contributed for decades can still be grouped into a single category. He pointed specifically to Canada, where he alleged that criminal activities linked to certain factions — including those associated with Khalistani networks — have begun to tarnish the image of the wider Indian community. His stated concern is collective punishment: the actions of a few leading to tighter policies that fall on Indians who followed legal pathways.

Context: a model under strain

Sareen argued that the current friction reflects a larger failure in how Western governments have managed cultural diversity, with the model of multiculturalism under significant strain and political systems struggling to address public anxiety over identity, employment and social cohesion. The episode's agenda ranged across assimilation and cultural integration, the sustainability of Europe's welfare state, whether immigration is becoming a race issue, and the future balance between labour needs and border controls. That last point is the structural tension: Western economies remain heavily reliant on foreign talent to fill labour shortages and offset ageing populations, even as governments face mounting political pressure to restrict entry.

Impact and what is next

For the diaspora, the exposure is practical before it is political. Policy shifts driven by a general backlash tend to arrive as more stringent visa requirements, longer scrutiny and greater uncertainty for people seeking to study or work abroad — and as a harder climate for those already settled. Sareen's warning is an assessment, not a policy announcement: no Western government has announced measures aimed at Indians as a group. What to watch is whether the rhetoric now running through debates in France, the United States and Britain hardens into rules — higher salary thresholds, tighter student and work routes, stricter enforcement — that change the terms on which the next generation of Indian migrants arrives, and on which the current one is judged.
